statement: Show that the equation $x^{3}+3x-5=0$ has exactly one real root. Use the Newton–Raphson method with starting value $x_{0}=1$ to find this root correct to three decimal places.
solution: Let $f(x)=x^{3}+3x-5$. Then $f'(x)=3x^{2}+3>0$ for all real $x$, so $f$ is strictly increasing and has at most one real root. Since $f(1)=-1<0$ and $f(2)=9>0$, there is exactly one real root in $(1,2)$. Newton's method gives $x_{1}=1-\dfrac{f(1)}{f'(1)}=1-\dfrac{-1}{6}=\tfrac76\approx1.1667$. Continuing, $x_{2}\approx1.1791$, $x_{3}\approx1.1545$, $x_{4}\approx1.1542$, so to three decimal places the root is $x\approx1.154$.
hints: Show $f'(x)>0$ so there is at most one root.
